newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish central bank says rate cut unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Polish central bank says rate cut unlikely.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said on Wednesday interest rates were relativley low and a rate move was unlikely in the near term.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said it was more likely the central bank would cut obligatory reserves than interest rates.
"Interest rates are relatively low and the central bank uses its interest rate policy to encourage savings," Gronkiewicz-Waltz told a news conference.
"The central bank is more likely to lower obligatory bank reserve levels than to lower interest rates," she added.

She said obligatory reserves, now at 17 percent for zloty call deposits and nine percent for term deposits, was the monetary policy instrument which the NBP planned to use more frequently than changes in interest rate levels.
The NBP last cut official interest rates by one point on July 16, with the lombard rate currently at 25 percent and the discount rate at 22 percent.
It cut reserves on zloty call deposits by three percentage points from the start of July.
Polish year-on-year inflation stands at 20.5 percent in August, up from 20.4 percent in July and down from 21.6 percent in December 1995.
Analysts expected prices to grow 1.4 percent in September, which could depress the year-on-year index to around 19 percent this month.
The central bank created obligatory reserves after several banks failed early in the decade when Poland was beginning its transition to a market economy.
